The space that opens is one you no longer have to manage, because nobody is being asked to carry the ending for you.

Let it stay small: a thing in your life that is genuinely done gets no more of tomorrow — off the list, out of the conversation. Keep up with the rest exactly as you have been. What's growing underneath gets more of you when you're no longer propping up what isn't. Care can be shown by removing attention, not only by giving it.
1.sheetLine: Let go of what's finished, gently and without a speech.

2.tense: You will keep handing things over before they have had time to be finished.
2.verb: Letting go of what no longer serves
2.place: In half-lit terrain, one step at a time
2.ask: Hold to a small practice daily this week, same time, same length, on the flat days and the pointless ones. Change nothing about it.
2.core:
In uncertain territory, you tend to release early. It looks like grace from the outside — stepping back before anyone asks you to, giving something up before it can be taken. Underneath, it's bracing: you let go of things that are still alive because finishing them would mean waiting to see how they turn out, and waiting is where the ache lives.

Keeping one small practice takes the opposite route. Do it on the flat days, the pointless days, the ones where nothing is moving. What you'll find is that staying with a thing while it's uncertain is a skill, not a sentence — and the release that comes after a real finish feels like setting something down rather than dropping it.
2.sheetLine: You release early to avoid the wait.

3.tense: You were still gripping what you had already set down, holding it long after it was over.
3.verb: Letting go of what no longer serves
3.place: In half-lit terrain, one step at a time
3.ask: Take something heavy you can't set down yet and carry it for the next hour without tightening around it. No fixing, no deciding. Just carry it.
3.core:
In fog, you keep your hands fixed on things that are long finished. A decision gets held a week past its life; an unfinished conversation gets rehearsed in case it matters again. The effort is invisible to most people, including you — it reads as being tired all the time, or as a grip that won't come off.

You don't have to release it all at once. For the next hour, carry what's heavy without adding force — don't grip it tighter, don't pretend it's not there. Keeping something at its real weight, for one hour, is a release in slow motion, and it's one your body can actually do. Stand in it a while longer and the grip loosens without your help.
3.sheetLine: You can carry what's heavy without gripping it.

4.tense: Something has already been let go of, and you are still talking as if you chose it.
4.verb: Letting go of what no longer serves
4.place: In half-lit terrain, one step at a time
4.ask: Give ten minutes of plain attention to something you actually want to keep, with no plan for it, the way you would water a young plant. Then stop.
4.core:
You've already set something down. The change is done — the old pattern isn't running, the decision is behind you — and your own account of it hasn't caught up. Other people have noticed the shift; you narrate it as if nothing has moved. The result is that you're caring for something no longer yours to carry, which costs more than finishing ever did.

Instead of auditing what you released, tend one thing that's still growing. Ten minutes of unplanned attention to something you actually want — the book, the walk, the person — tells you by contact what's still here. Care given to what's alive, with no schedule attached, shows you what you've already let go of, and you don't have to decide anything about it to see it.
4.sheetLine: You've already let go. Your account hasn't caught up.

1.tense: You are done with something, and you are letting it go from here.
1.verb: letting go of a grip on purpose, once what it was holding is finished
1.place: where you're becoming what you already are
1.ask: Clear the hours or the shelf that a finished thing was taking, and leave the space open. Don't plan the replacement — just let whatever grows there grow.
1.core:
Something in your life has finished, and you're putting it down without calling it a defeat. You can feel the difference between setting something down and having it torn out of your hands. This is the first one. There's a lightness in your body where the grip used to be, and you're not rushing to fill the space. That's the mechanism working — what you are shows more clearly because less is covering it.

The next step keeps the balance from sliding back: clear the hours or the shelf a finished thing was taking, and leave the space open. Don't plan the replacement. Let whatever grows there grow. This is the part people skip. You won't skip it — you'll notice nothing has to be pushed into the space, and the space stays yours.
1.sheetLine: You put it down. The space is yours, not a wound.

2.tense: You will be finished with things before they are done, and you will call it release.
2.verb: letting go of a grip on purpose, once what it was holding is finished
2.place: where you're becoming what you already are
2.ask: Before you release anything this week, do the plain version of it once — the smallest real piece, not the plan — then decide whether it's actually finished.
2.core:
You're releasing things ahead of their time, and releasing has started to look like a performance. A thing is barely underway and you've already let it go — quit the class, ended the arrangement, called it finished. There's a story in it about surrender, but from outside it reads as leaving before anyone could measure you. You're braced for a future you can't write, so you keep making endings you can control.

What's thin is follow-through, not release. Keep a small practice alive instead — alone, repeated, unglamorous. Before you let anything go this week, do the plain version of it once: the smallest real piece, not your plan for it. Then decide, with that behind you, whether it's actually finished. Most things won't be. The ones that are, you'll release for real, and you'll know the difference.
2.sheetLine: You're quitting things to finish them. Do one small piece first.

3.tense: You stood at a door for too long, and the room behind you has already moved on.
3.verb: letting go of a grip on purpose, once what it was holding is finished
3.place: where you're becoming what you already are
3.ask: Bear something you're still holding that's already over, without deciding anything about it — no plan to drop it, no digging into why. Stay standing there a while.
3.core:
You're holding onto something long past its end, and it's gone into your body — shoulders, jaw, the low ache that doesn't quite leave. Keeping your grip on has become the daily work, as if it might still need you. It hasn't for a while. The tiredness isn't from the load. It's from the tightening.

What's empty is your strength to hold, not your strength to release. Build the stronger standing first. Bear something you're still clutching that's already finished, without deciding anything about it — no plan to drop it, no digging into why you haven't. Let it sit as it is. Stay standing with it a while. Your grip eases once you stop asking it to hold the entire weight.
3.sheetLine: You're not failing to let go. You're gripping too hard to feel it.

4.tense: You have already let something go, and you are still talking about it as if you hadn't.
4.verb: letting go of a grip on purpose, once what it was holding is finished
4.place: where you're becoming what you already are
4.ask: Look after something alive right now — a habit, a person, a patch of work — by what today asks for, not by what its schedule says. Expect nothing back.
4.core:
Something has already ended, and part of you has already let it go — but your story and your hands don't agree. You describe it as ongoing, as something you're still keeping. Meanwhile you've quietly stopped showing up; the release is done and unsigned. It runs the other way too: sometimes you insist you're at peace with something you're still clutching. Either way, the one doing the moving isn't watching.

The next move is small and physical. Look after something alive right now — a habit, a person, a patch of work — by what today asks for, not by what its schedule says. Show up without forcing a result. The point isn't the growing thing. It's that you'll catch your own hands at work: your attention, your choice, your timing. Say what you've already released. Say what you haven't. That's the whole act, and it's enough.
4.sheetLine: You already let it go. Your story just hasn't caught up.

1.tense: The release is already under way and you are here with it, not bracing.
1.verb: letting go of what no longer serves, on purpose
1.place: standing outside the system while still inside it, seeing the whole pattern at once
1.ask: Look for the least of what you've already set down and tend it today — your care, nothing asked back.
1.core:
Something finished nearby — a role, a routine, a version of yourself — and you put it down without making a story of it. Release comes after the finishing, not instead of it, and you can tell finishing from quitting. You see the whole pattern and stay inside it anyway.

What feeds this next is care that doesn't clutch. Take the least of what you've already set down, the piece still close enough to touch, and give it your attention today with nothing asked back. Care that doesn't grip is what keeps release from wearing you out. Whatever else is mid-finish will arrive at its own ending, and you'll be here watching it.
1.sheetLine: What finished is behind you, and you're still here.

2.tense: You will be releasing something next before it has actually finished.
2.verb: letting go of what no longer serves, on purpose
2.place: standing outside the system while still inside it, seeing the whole pattern at once
2.ask: When the pull comes to exit something early, run the plain version of it once more that day — same shape, on your own — and stay in it even when it bores.
2.core:
From outside the pattern you can see endings before they arrive, and that sight has started to hurry your hand. You step back from things ahead of their finish — leaving roles, giving up before the effort can be weighed — and it can look like humility. Underneath, release has turned into a way of avoiding the completion of anything. The whole pattern is still visible. What's missing is the part where a thing runs to its end first.

What steadies this is repetition kept dull on purpose. When the pull comes to exit something early, run the plain version once more that same day — same shape, on your own — and stay in it even when it bores. Finishing the boring round teaches your hand the difference between completing and quitting. The predictable repetition will hold you still long enough for the thing to end before you leave.
2.sheetLine: You are letting go before the thing is finished.

3.tense: You have been holding something and are still standing at that door.
3.verb: letting go of what no longer serves, on purpose
3.place: standing outside the system while still inside it, seeing the whole pattern at once
3.ask: Take what you're still carrying and stand in it a while more without deciding anything — no setting down, no tightening.
3.core:
You can see the whole pattern in a situation and still not put anything down. Some grip you took up is still in your hands, and the watching has become part of it — you see the situation from outside and keep your weight on it anyway. The tiredness isn't from the load. It's from staying clenched around it, unable to set something down without feeling like you're abandoning it.

Here's another way to move. Take what you're carrying and stand in it a while more without doing anything with it — hold your shape, ask nothing of yourself, make no decision, don't set it down. You're practicing the difference between bearing something and gripping it. For one hour you can be the one who holds it steady instead of the one who won't set it down.
3.sheetLine: You can see the whole thing and still not set it down.

4.tense: You have already released something and are reading the room as if nothing has moved.
4.verb: letting go of what no longer serves, on purpose
4.place: standing outside the system while still inside it, seeing the whole pattern at once
4.ask: Whatever you keep coming back to, leave space around it and don't steer it — no result, no direction, just the room.
4.core:
Something you already let go of — or are still carrying in a way you haven't let yourself notice — and you see the pattern well enough that the release feels like it happened to you rather than through you. From inside, it looks like the situation changed and you adapted. From outside, it looks like you made a choice and haven't claimed it. Either way you're standing in the middle of it without recognizing your own hand.

Leave it some room. Whatever you keep coming back to, give it space and don't steer it — no push, no finish, no judgment. Just the room. That teaches you something either way: whether you already let go and haven't admitted it, or didn't and are still holding. Making room without steering is what release feels like once it's recognized.
4.sheetLine: You've already let go, or you haven't, and you aren't claiming it.

1.tense: The release comes when the work is finished, not before and not after.
1.verb: Letting go on purpose when something is finished
1.place: At the threshold where a work is complete and the next step begins
1.ask: A job on the bench is done. Ask what it actually wants today — a last look, or the shelf — and follow that answer instead of a plan that says it should still be getting something. Needing nothing is a real answer.
1.core:
When a piece of work reaches its natural end, you set it down without grimacing. The last stroke lands, the grip eases, and you cross into whatever is next. You don't drag the finished thing along to prove you earned the rest. You give the next thing room by closing this one.

Walk one ending through this week where another person can see it happen. Not a report, not a goodbye speech — the plain act of stopping, done in view. A finished thing set down while someone watches shows them how an ending goes when nobody is performing. Don't explain it after.
1.sheetLine: You can end a thing without calling it a loss.

2.tense: The ending will be hurried, because staying until it is finished feels like it might never arrive.
2.verb: Letting go on purpose when something is finished
2.place: At the threshold where a work is complete and the next step begins
2.ask: You'd rather walk off before it finishes. Do the plain, unglamorous version instead — the smallest complete form. No upgrade, no announcement, no exit speech. The belated finish may sting more than bolting would have.
2.core:
When something nears its end, you can release it a beat early — call it over before it has actually ended, skip the last turn because the finish already feels late. You leave first, so nothing gets to leave you. What's skipped is the piece that would have made the closing clean.

Take the plain ending before you improvise a bigger one. Finish the thing at the size it actually is, not at the size your story about it demands. Let it be small and complete rather than large and abandoned. The person who watches doesn't need the drama, and neither do you.
2.sheetLine: You end it early so the ending can't reach you.

3.tense: The grip stays closed on a thing that finished, and the arm holding it has gone sore.
3.verb: Letting go on purpose when something is finished
3.place: At the threshold where a work is complete and the next step begins
3.ask: Your hand keeps ahold of a weight without you deciding to. Stay through one ordinary hour of it and settle nothing. Don't force the drop, don't plan it. Nobody says the hand must open — only notice you're still holding on.
3.core:
The ending came, and the hands are still closed around something that already stopped being yours to carry. What was going to be set down stayed held, and now that is the work — kept so steadily the shoulders have forgotten they could drop. Releasing isn't refused here — it has simply dropped out of the available moves.

Don't sit down to practice release. Stand through the next hour without settling one thing about it. The following work will begin when it begins, and until then, holding at the true size is enough. That tightness is not a verdict on who you are. It's a grip that hasn't heard the news yet.
3.sheetLine: Your hand still holds what already ended.

4.tense: You have already put it down, and you still tell the story as if you were carrying it.
4.verb: Letting go on purpose when something is finished
4.place: At the threshold where a work is complete and the next step begins
4.ask: One story you tell about a hard stretch has an ending you actually reached, not the one you repeat. Go back to that finished thing, name what changed, once, and skip the bow after.
4.core:
When you finish with something and truly leave it finished, you don't turn back to check its weight. The hands are empty, and you walk toward what's next without a backward narration. Done means done, and you can feel that the way you feel a room when the noise stops.

In one story you tell about a hard season, the ending you actually reached is already there — but you file it under what happened to you, or under the fight, or under nothing at all. Go back to that ending with nothing added. Sit with one hard thing you finished, name what changed, plain, once. The plainest version is the true one.
4.sheetLine: You already let it go. The telling hasn't caught up.
